conceptTag: Should a founder do their own bookkeeping?
readerTitle: Should you do your own books? Price your hours first
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 소매점, 비스트로) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 적용 레슨: 기회비용과 비교우위
insight: 직접 하면 공짜인 일은 없다. 그 시간에 할 수 있었던 더 가치 있는 일이 진짜 비용이고, 일은 포기하는 것이 가장 적은 사람에게 맡긴다.
misconception: 내가 직접 하면 돈이 안 든다. 내가 제일 잘하는 일이면 내가 해야 한다.

factChecks.note: 소매점 계산: 직접 하면 6시간 × 시간당 매장 매출총이익 $60 = $360 포기. 북키퍼 3시간 × $40 = $120. 차이 $360 − $120 = $240/주. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
5번 카드의 '마야가 2시간에 끝낸다'는 가정에는 숫자 계산을 붙이지 않았습니다. 시간당 $60 기준이면 $120로 북키퍼 비용과 같아져 비교우위 설명이 흐려지기 때문입니다. 숫자를 추가하려면 이 점을 다시 확인하세요.
특정 국가의 세무·회계 규정은 다루지 않았습니다. 장부 위탁 시 법적 책임에 관한 문구는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The free bookkeeper who costs the most
body: It's 10 p.m. on a Sunday. Maya runs a small home-goods shop, and she's at her kitchen table matching receipts to bank lines.
She does her own books because a bookkeeper costs money and she doesn't. At least, that's how it looks.

image.label: Shop owner at a kitchen table late at night with receipts
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤늦은 부엌 식탁, 영수증 더미와 노트북 앞에 앉은 소매점 주인. 창밖은 어둡고 벽시계는 10시. 식탁 한쪽에 매장 열쇠와 앞치마. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Keep the books, or hand them off?
body: Maya spends about 6 hours a week on the books. A local bookkeeper would do the same work in 3 hours at $40 an hour.
On busy Saturdays, each hour Maya spends on the shop floor brings in about $60 of extra gross profit (sales minus the cost of the goods). What should she do?

options.text: Keep doing it herself. That saves $120 a week
options.feedback: This counts the cash she'd spend but not the time she gives up. That's **opportunity cost**: her 6 hours could bring in about $360 on the floor.

options.text: Hire the bookkeeper and move those hours to the shop floor
options.feedback: She pays $120 and gains about $360. Pricing her own hours by **opportunity cost** makes the bookkeeper the cheaper option.

options.text: Hire the bookkeeper and take Sunday evenings off
options.feedback: Rest has real value, and it's a fair trade if she chooses it on purpose. In money terms, though, she pays $120 and earns nothing back.

cards.title: Same week, two ways to do the books.
body: The bookkeeper looks like the expensive option until you put a price on Maya's hours.

breakdown.label: Cash cost, doing it herself
breakdown.detail: What shows up in the bank

breakdown.label: Better off each week
breakdown.detail: By handing off and selling instead

cards.title: Your time has a price, even when nobody sends a bill.
body: **Opportunity cost** is the value of the best thing you give up when you choose something else.
Maya's bookkeeping never shows up as an expense. But it costs her the Saturday sales she isn't making. The useful question isn't "Can I do this myself?" It's "What else would these hours do?"

cards.title: What if Maya is faster than the bookkeeper?
body: Say Maya used to work in accounting and could finish the books in 2 hours. She's faster than anyone she could hire. Should she keep them?

Not necessarily. **Comparative advantage** says a task goes to whoever gives up the least to do it, not whoever does it best. Maya is a bit better at books, and much better at selling than any bookkeeper. Her edge is biggest on the floor, so that's where her hours belong.

image.label: Two people, two tasks, arrows showing who gives up less
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 매장 주인, 오른쪽에 북키퍼. 가운데 두 과제 아이콘 "Books"와 "Selling". 주인에게서 "Selling"으로 굵은 화살표, 북키퍼에게서 "Books"로 화살표. 상단에 "Who gives up less?" 문구.

cards.softwareNote: A software founder who writes the best code on the team may still do more good on sales calls, if several people can ship features but no one else can close deals.

cards.title: Handing off isn't the same as looking away.
body: The saving is real only if the freed hours go to something worth more. If Maya spends them on email, the $120 fee buys nothing.

Doing the books yourself for the first few months can teach you where the money goes. After you hand them off, keep reading a short monthly summary and check it against the bank. Handing off also takes setup time, and mistakes in someone else's work are still your problem.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: Sam is the chef-owner of a 40-seat bistro. He's faster than anyone on his staff at both cooking and spreadsheets. His afternoons go to prep and testing new dishes.
His floor manager, Lena, is slower with the books but has quiet time from 3 to 5 p.m. most days. Who should do the weekly books?

options.feedback: He'd save bookkeeping time but lose prep and menu work only he can do. Being best at a task isn't the same as having a **comparative advantage** in it.

options.text: Lena, in her quiet afternoons, with Sam reviewing a one-page summary
options.feedback: Lena's quiet hours have a low **opportunity cost**, and Sam stays in the kitchen. The summary keeps him close to food and labor costs.

options.text: An outside bookkeeper, and Sam stops looking at the numbers
options.feedback: It frees everyone's time for a fee. But a restaurant can lose money fast without anyone noticing, so giving up the review is a costly trade.

cards.title: Price your hours before you call a task free.
body: Two ideas from this unit did the work today:
list: **Opportunity cost** (ECO-01-03): a task you do yourself costs whatever those hours could earn elsewhere
**Comparative advantage** (ECO-01-06): give each task to the person who gives up the least to do it
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list three tasks you do every week. Next to each, write what an hour of your time could earn elsewhere and what it would cost to hand the task off.
